analogy.p: Think of the Earth's temperature as the water level in a bath. The tap is the radiation absorbed from the Sun and the plug hole is the radiation emitted to space. If the tap runs faster than the water drains, the level rises (warming); if the drain is faster, the level falls (cooling); if they match, the level stays steady. A bath drains faster when it is deeper, just as a hotter Earth emits more, which is why the level settles at a new steady value. Greenhouse gases are like partly blocking the plug hole. The analogy breaks down because water is a material that is physically stored, whereas the Earth stores thermal energy and radiation can cross empty space.
analogy.t: A bath with the tap running and the plug out

bullets: **Reflected**: the radiation bounces off and returns the way it came; the energy is not absorbed so it does **not** warm the object.
**Absorbed**: the energy of the radiation is transferred to the object, usually increasing its **thermal store**, so it warms up.
**Transmitted**: radiation passes through, for example visible light through clear glass or air.
Light-coloured, shiny surfaces (snow, ice, clouds) are good **reflectors**; dark, matt surfaces (forests, dark rock, oceans) are good **absorbers**.
The atmosphere is largely **transparent** to visible light from the Sun but **absorbs** some infrared wavelengths.
Every radiation question should say which of the three happens and where.
core.h: Radiation can be reflected, absorbed or transmitted
core.p: When electromagnetic radiation meets a surface or a boundary, it can be **reflected** (bounces back), **absorbed** (its energy is transferred to the material, usually warming it) or **transmitted** (passes through). Which of these happens depends on the **material** and on the **wavelength** of the radiation. This idea is the foundation of every question about the temperature of the Earth, because the Earth's surface, clouds, ice, oceans and atmosphere all treat different radiations in different ways.

bullets: **All bodies (objects) emit radiation**; the hotter the body, the more energy it emits each second.
Emission is the transfer of energy by **infrared radiation** (and other wavelengths if very hot), needing no medium; it can cross a vacuum.
Everyday objects at room temperature mainly emit **infrared**, which we cannot see.
Very hot objects such as the Sun emit visible light, ultraviolet and infrared.
Absorption and emission are happening at the same time; what matters is which is **greater**.
This applies to a cup of tea, a person, the Moon, and the Earth.
core.h: All objects absorb and emit radiation
core.p: Every object **emits** electromagnetic radiation (mostly infrared at everyday temperatures) and also **absorbs** radiation from its surroundings, all the time. This is true whether the object is hot or cold. The **hotter** the object, the more radiation it emits in each second. So the temperature of any body is decided by the balance between the **radiation it absorbs** and the **radiation it emits**.

bullets: Rate of absorption > rate of emission: temperature **rises**.
Rate of absorption < rate of emission: temperature **falls**.
Rate of absorption = rate of emission: temperature is **constant** (equilibrium).
Use the exam wording: 'the Earth absorbs radiation at a greater rate than it emits it'.
Because emission rises with temperature, a body that warms emits more until the two rates match again, which is a self-balancing effect.
The same logic explains why a cold object left in a warm room warms up (it absorbs more than it emits) until it reaches a steady temperature.
core.h: The balance rule: what happens to temperature
core.p: The central rule for this topic is that the **temperature of a body is related to the balance between the incoming radiation it absorbs and the radiation it emits**. If a body absorbs radiation **faster** than it emits it, its temperature **increases**. If it emits faster than it absorbs, its temperature **decreases**. If the two rates are equal, the temperature stays **constant**. Always talk about **rates** (energy per second), not just 'amount'.

bullets: Constant temperature: **rate of absorption = rate of emission**.
The body is still absorbing and emitting; the net change in thermal energy is zero.
The Earth as a whole is approximately in balance over long periods, so average temperatures are fairly stable.
If something changes the balance (reflectivity, atmosphere, Sun), the Earth warms or cools until a **new balance** is reached at a new temperature.
The new equilibrium temperature is reached because emission increases (or decreases) as temperature changes.
Do not say 'the Earth stops absorbing'; say the rates are equal.
core.p: A body at a **constant temperature** is absorbing radiation at exactly the same rate as it is emitting. It does not mean that nothing is happening: energy is still arriving and leaving, but the **net transfer is zero**. The Earth is close to this situation on average over a year, so its average temperature is roughly steady, although it fluctuates between day and night and between seasons.

bullets: Hotter body: **greater intensity** of radiation emitted at every wavelength.
Hotter body: the **peak wavelength** is **shorter**.
The Sun (very hot surface) has its peak intensity in the **visible** part of the spectrum.
The Earth (about 15 degrees Celsius on average) emits mainly **infrared**.
This difference in wavelength is the key to the greenhouse effect: the atmosphere treats the two radiations differently.
Graphs of intensity against wavelength show a hump; a hotter body gives a taller hump further to the left.
core.p: Both the **intensity** (how much radiation is emitted per second) and the **wavelength distribution** (which wavelengths) of the radiation depend on the temperature of the body. As a body gets hotter, the **total intensity** emitted increases, and the **peak wavelength** moves towards shorter wavelengths. This is why the very hot Sun mainly emits visible light and UV, while the much cooler Earth emits mostly **infrared**, which has a longer wavelength.

bullets: Incoming radiation is mainly **visible light** with some UV and infrared.
Some is **reflected into space** by clouds, ice, snow, deserts and the atmosphere (roughly 30% overall).
Some is **absorbed by the atmosphere**, for example UV absorbed by the ozone layer.
The rest is **absorbed by the Earth's surface** (land and oceans), increasing thermal energy.
Without absorption by the surface the Earth would stay far colder.
The surface warming is the main source of heating of the lower atmosphere.
core.h: The Earth's incoming radiation from the Sun
core.p: The Earth receives radiation from the Sun, mostly **visible light**, with some **ultraviolet** and **infrared**. This is short-wavelength radiation relative to what the Earth itself emits. Not all of it reaches the surface and not all of it is absorbed: some is **reflected** back into space by clouds, the atmosphere and bright surfaces; some is **absorbed** by the atmosphere (for example ozone absorbs much of the UV); and the rest reaches the surface where most of it is **absorbed**, warming the land and oceans.

bullets: More **cloud cover** or **ice** gives more reflection, so a **lower** absorbed rate and cooling.
Melting ice exposes dark ocean or land, which **absorbs** more, so warming increases (a **positive feedback** idea).
Volcanic ash and some particles reflect sunlight, which can cause short-term cooling.
Reflected radiation keeps its short wavelength and escapes to space.
Say clearly: 'less radiation is absorbed, so the rate of absorption falls below the rate of emission'.
A common mistake is to say reflected heat 'warms the atmosphere'; reflected radiation leaves.
core.p: The temperature of the Earth depends on **reflection of radiation into space**, because reflected radiation is never absorbed and so cannot warm the planet. Clouds, ice sheets, snow and light-coloured surfaces reflect a large fraction, which cools the planet. If the proportion reflected increases, the Earth absorbs less, so the balance shifts and the planet cools until a new, lower equilibrium is reached. If it decreases, the Earth absorbs more and warms.

bullets: Surface emits **infrared** because it is warm.
**Greenhouse gases** absorb infrared radiation and re-emit it in all directions, including back towards the surface.
Without this effect the average temperature would be well below freezing (roughly minus 18 degrees Celsius rather than about 15 degrees Celsius).
The atmosphere is transparent to most incoming visible light but not to outgoing infrared.
More greenhouse gas means more of the outgoing infrared is absorbed and returned, so the surface warms.
Link to **chemistry** (Earth's atmosphere and climate change) and **biology** (ecosystem effects).
core.h: Absorption and emission by the surface and atmosphere
core.p: The Earth's surface absorbs the Sun's short-wavelength radiation and warms. Because it is warm, the surface emits **infrared radiation** (long wavelength). Some of this infrared passes through the atmosphere into space, but some is **absorbed by greenhouse gases** such as carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour. The atmosphere then **re-emits** infrared in all directions, and some of it is sent back down to the surface, giving extra warming. This is why the Earth's average surface temperature is higher than it would be with no atmosphere.

bullets: **Daytime**: absorbed rate > emitted rate, so warming.
**Night**: emitted rate > absorbed rate, so cooling.
The highest temperature comes in the **afternoon** and the lowest near **dawn**, where the curves cross.
**Clouds** at night act like a blanket, absorbing and re-emitting infrared, so nights are warmer; clear nights are colder.
**Seasons** change the angle and duration of sunlight, which changes the absorbed rate.
Sea and land warm at different rates; link to specific heat capacity.
core.h: Day and night, seasons and local changes
core.p: Even in a stable climate the temperature of a place changes because the balance changes. By day the surface absorbs strong radiation from the Sun, so absorption exceeds emission and the temperature rises. At night there is no incoming sunlight, but the surface keeps emitting infrared, so emission exceeds absorption and it cools. The temperature peaks in the afternoon rather than exactly at midday, because the surface keeps warming while absorption is still greater than emission, and is lowest around dawn.

bullets: **More greenhouse gases** (from burning fossil fuels, deforestation): more infrared is absorbed and re-emitted downwards, so **emission to space falls** and the Earth warms.
**Less ice and snow**: less reflection, more absorption, warming.
**More cloud** (day): more reflection, cooling; (night): more infrared returned, warming.
**Volcanic eruptions**: particles in the upper atmosphere reflect sunlight and may cool the Earth for a short time.
**Changes in the Sun's output** or the Earth's orbit change the rate of incoming radiation.
In each case use cause then effect then new equilibrium.
core.h: Changing the balance: factors that can alter Earth's temperature
core.p: Any factor that changes the rate of absorption or emission, or the amount reflected into space, will change the average temperature until a new balance is reached. Natural factors include changes in volcanic activity and cloud cover; human activities change the amount of greenhouse gas, the amount of ice and forest, and the reflectivity of the land. Exam answers should name the factor and then say which of the three processes (reflection, absorption, emission) changes, and what that does to the balance.

bullets: Check wavelengths: arrows from the Sun are **short wavelength**; arrows from the Earth are **infrared (long wavelength)**.
Add up arrows: absorbed = incoming - reflected.
At equilibrium, total absorbed = total emitted.
On a graph of intensity against wavelength, the **area** relates to the total power emitted.
If the question says 'constant temperature', do not give an increase or decrease.
If asked to **draw** a diagram, include the Sun, atmosphere, surface, and labelled arrows for incoming, reflected, absorbed and emitted radiation, with 'short wavelength' and 'infrared' labels.
core.p: Exams often give a radiation diagram with arrows labelled with numbers or percentages, or a graph of intensity against wavelength. For diagrams, check each arrow: is it incoming or outgoing, short or long wavelength, reflected, absorbed or emitted? For data, use **conservation of energy**: at constant temperature, the energy absorbed equals the energy emitted. For graphs, remember that the hotter body has the taller curve, shifted to shorter wavelength.

exam: State the rule: temperature depends on the balance between the rate of absorption and the rate of emission of radiation.
For 'explain why temperature is constant', write 'rate of absorption equals rate of emission'.
For 'explain why temperature increases', write 'absorbs radiation at a greater rate than it emits it'.
For reflection: 'reflected into space so less radiation is absorbed'.
For greenhouse gases: 'absorb infrared radiation emitted by the Earth and re-emit it in all directions, some back towards the surface'.
Always mention wavelength: incoming is mainly visible light; outgoing is infrared.
For 4 and 6 mark questions, structure as: source, what happens (reflect/absorb/emit), effect on rates, effect on temperature, new equilibrium.
For diagrams: label arrows with 'incoming (short wavelength)', 'reflected', 'absorbed' and 'emitted infrared'.
Graphs: hotter = taller curve and peak at shorter wavelength.
Use the words rate or power, not just 'amount' or 'heat'.
Check whether the question is about the whole Earth over time, or about a place over a day.

mistakes.r: At constant temperature the Earth absorbs radiation at the same rate as it emits it.
mistakes.w: The Earth's temperature stays the same because it stops absorbing radiation.

mistakes.r: They absorb infrared and re-emit it in all directions, so less escapes to space and some is returned to the surface.
mistakes.w: Greenhouse gases trap heat so none gets out.

mistakes.r: The Sun emits mainly visible light (short wavelength); the Earth emits infrared (longer wavelength).
mistakes.w: The Sun's radiation and the Earth's radiation are the same wavelength.

mistakes.r: Reflected radiation is not absorbed, so it does not warm the Earth; it goes back into space.
All objects emit radiation, and hotter objects emit more.
The surface keeps warming while absorbed rate exceeds emitted rate, so it peaks in the afternoon.
mistakes.w: Temperature is hottest at noon because the Sun is highest.

mistakes.r: Radiation from the Sun crosses empty space; conduction and convection need particles.
mistakes.w: The Earth gets heat by conduction from the Sun.

mistakes.r: Ice reflects radiation, so more ice means less absorbed and cooling.
mistakes.w: More ice means a warmer Earth.

summary: You need to explain how the temperature of the Earth depends on the balance between the rates at which it absorbs and emits radiation and on the reflection of radiation into space, and to interpret and draw diagrams of these energy transfers (physics only). It matters because the same balance idea explains day and night, the greenhouse effect and climate change.

terms.d: Radiation is absorbed when its energy is transferred to the material, usually increasing its thermal store.
Radiation is reflected when it bounces off a surface rather than entering it.
Radiation is transmitted when it passes through a material.
To give out electromagnetic radiation; all objects emit radiation.
Electromagnetic radiation emitted by all objects; the Earth emits mainly infrared.
The power (energy per second) of radiation per unit area; hotter objects emit radiation of greater intensity.
The wavelength at which an object emits the greatest intensity; shorter for hotter objects.
When rate of absorption equals rate of emission so temperature stays constant.
A gas in the atmosphere that absorbs infrared radiation and re-emits it in all directions, such as carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour.
The energy store of an object related to its temperature; increases when it absorbs more than it emits.
The layer of gases around the Earth.
The amount of energy absorbed or emitted per second (power).
The distance between a point on a wave and the same point on the next wave.

worked.q: For every 100 units of radiation reaching the Earth from the Sun, 30 units are reflected to space. Assume the Earth is at constant temperature. How many units does it emit? (2 marks)
steps: At constant temperature the rate of absorption equals the rate of emission.

worked.ans: Absorbed is 65 and emitted is 70, so the Earth cools until a new, lower equilibrium temperature.
worked.q: Following a large increase in snow cover, 35 of every 100 units are now reflected. Compare absorbed and emitted radiation at first (emission still 70) and state what happens to temperature. (3 marks)
steps: The Earth loses more than it gains, so cools and emits less until emission = 65.

worked.ans: The Earth absorbs radiation from the Sun at the same rate as it emits radiation to space, so its temperature stays roughly constant. The surface absorbs short-wavelength radiation and emits infrared. Greenhouse gases absorb infrared and re-emit it in all directions, some back to the surface. If there are more greenhouse gases, less infrared escapes, so the Earth absorbs radiation at a greater rate than it emits it to space and the temperature rises until emission equals absorption at a higher temperature.
worked.q: Explain why the Earth's temperature remains roughly constant, and how an increase in greenhouse gases would change it. (6 marks)
steps: Constant: rate of absorption equals rate of emission.
Visible light from the Sun is absorbed by the surface; the surface emits infrared.
Greenhouse gases absorb infrared and re-emit it in all directions, including downwards.
More greenhouse gas means less infrared escapes, so emitted rate to space is less than absorbed rate.
Temperature rises until emission to space equals absorption again at a higher temperature.
